description: Team FirstBeat is working on a problem every future Mars crew will face: when Earth is up to 22 minutes away by radio, there’s no live doctor to ask when something feels wrong with your heart. Every question costs a round trip of about 44 minutes. We’re building a decision-support tool that learns each astronaut’s own baseline, flags early changes, guides the next step, and prepares a summary for Earth, so the crew has a plan while they wait for a reply.
summary:
FirstBeat is a heart-health decision-support prototype for future Mars crews. On a Mars transit, radio messages take up to about 22 minutes each way, so there’s no live doctor to ask. FirstBeat gives the crew their first five minutes of help.

It learns each astronaut’s own baseline and flags when their readings drift, such as a rising resting heart rate over three days. A short guided check-in then recommends a clear next step, from resting and rechecking to acting immediately for warning symptoms. It also prepares a summary of the baseline, trend, symptoms, and advice for the first message to Earth.

The prototype includes a crew dashboard and a simulated onboard server that updates it live, and it keeps working during an outage. Solar events on the timeline come from NASA’s DONKI space weather data. The logic is rule-based, so it can run offline on board.

Crew vitals are simulated, and the questions and thresholds are placeholders for flight surgeons to validate. It is decision support, not diagnosis.
details:
FirstBeat is a heart-health decision-support prototype for future Mars crews. On a Mars transit, radio messages take up to about 22 minutes each way, so a live doctor can’t answer in time. FirstBeat learns each astronaut’s own baseline from their first 24 days of readings (resting heart rate, blood pressure, sleep, and exercise) and flags a sustained drift, such as three days of rising resting heart rate. A short guided check-in then recommends a next step, from resting and rechecking to acting immediately if warning symptoms appear. It also prepares a summary of the baseline, trend, symptoms, and advice, so the first message to Earth already has what a doctor needs.

The prototype is built with plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with a hand-drawn SVG chart and a design made in Figma. A simulated onboard server feeds the dashboard live and keeps it working from a saved copy during an outage. Solar events on the timeline come from NASA’s DONKI space weather data. Because the logic is rule-based, it can run offline and is easy to explain and audit. Its creative angle is focusing on one organ and one scenario, treating the 44-minute round trip as a design requirement and not an afterthought. The goal is to help future crews handle early heart-health changes on their own, and the same approach could support remote clinics, ships, and polar stations on Earth.

The crew vitals are simulated, and the questions and thresholds are placeholders for flight surgeons to validate. It is decision support, not diagnosis.
dataRefs: NASA DONKI (Space Weather Database Of Notifications, Knowledge, Information)
projectRefs: Risk of Cardiovascular Adaptations Contributing to Adverse Mission Performance and Health Outcomes (CV Risk)
